caption:
United Airlines is banning unauthorized AI agents from booking flights for travelers, on its own site and through travel agencies.
The airline says bots with your login could make purchases you did not want or spend your MileagePlus miles.
AI tools can still show United's flights and fares, they just cannot finish the booking.

Would you let an AI agent book your flights?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: CBS News, Air Data News · Photo: Air Data News
threads_text: United Airlines just banned unauthorized AI agents from booking its flights, even through travel agencies. The airline says a bot with your login could buy tickets or burn your miles without you meaning to. Would you trust an AI agent with your airline account?

site_article.headline: United Airlines bans unauthorized AI agents from booking flights for travelers
site_article.dek: The airline says personal AI assistants could expose account data, make unwanted purchases or spend MileagePlus miles, and it will block them on its own channels and through travel agencies.
site_article.summary: United Airlines said on November 11, 2026, that it will prohibit unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights on travelers' behalf. The restriction covers United's website and app as well as travel agencies and aggregators, while AI tools may still display United's flights and fares.
site_article.seo_title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights
site_article.seo_description: United will block unauthorized AI agents from booking its flights on its site, its app and through travel agencies, citing security and federal rules.
site_article.answer_summary: Unauthorized AI agents such as personal AI assistants can no longer complete United Airlines bookings for travelers, either on United's own platforms or through travel agencies. They can still show United flights and fares.

paragraphs.text: United Airlines said on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, that it will ban unauthorized third-party AI agents and assistants from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, according to CBS News. The airline is updating its booking, ticketing and distribution policies to put the rule into effect, Air Data News reported.

The restriction applies to United's own digital platforms and also to indirect channels, meaning travel agencies and ticket aggregators. According to Air Data News, the policy does not stop AI assistants from showing United's flights and fares; it stops them from completing reservations through the airline's systems without authorization. United did not announce a specific timetable for enforcement.
CBS News cited Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots as examples of the consumer AI agents that have started to book travel and handle other tasks for their users.

United's main argument is security. The airline said that sharing account credentials with personal third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and that actions taken by these tools can lead to purchases, account changes or use of MileagePlus miles that the customer did not intend, according to CBS News and Air Data News.

The airline also pointed to federal rules. At check-in, passengers must confirm that their luggage contains no prohibited items, and United said letting an agent handle that step without the traveler's direct confirmation could conflict with those requirements. Air Data News reported that United plans to update its Digital Trust Center to explain the change and to help customers affected by unintended actions taken by AI assistants.

Reservations completed by such tools before November 11 will be honored, according to Travel Weekly as cited by Air Data News. The airline said it will keep evaluating how third-party AI tools interact with its services, which leaves room for authorizing specific platforms later.

United chief executive Scott Kirby said at an event in Chicago on November 10 that he did not want to create another intermediary between the airline and its customers, The Wall Street Journal reported, as cited by Air Data News. Henry Harteveldt of Atmosphere Research Group told CBS News that the policy suggests United wants to keep control of the booking process, and that it likely also wants to avoid the costs of a surge in flight searches run by AI bots.

Other carriers are taking a different approach. Delta Air Lines has indicated that properly authenticated AI assistants can make reservations, with additional safeguards for sensitive transactions, according to Air Data News. Southwest Airlines has made its flight inventory available to ChatGPT users. Harteveldt told CBS News that United fares can still be booked through Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights.

The decision draws a clear line between AI tools that help travelers search and AI tools that act inside a customer's account. United is leaving the first kind alone and closing the door on the second unless it has approved the platform, which keeps the airline in charge of the final sale and of the data that comes with it.
The next signal is whether United authorizes any specific AI platform to book on its systems, and whether other large carriers follow its approach or Delta's.
